15730:
To talk someone into something means to persuade or convince a person to do something they were not originally planning to do — using words, reasons, or arguments.

In simple terms: You use your words to change someone's mind until they agree to do something.
Breaking It Down Word by Word

Think of it like this:

  • "Talk" — you are using spoken words (or sometimes written words)
  • "into" — this word signals movement — you are moving someone into a decision or action
  • "something" — the action or thing you want them to do

So the full picture is: you are verbally pushing someone into doing something. It's like using your words as a tool to open a door and guide someone through it.
The Grammar Structure

This idiom always follows this pattern:

talk + [person] + into + [doing something]

The word after "into" is always a verb ending in -ing (a gerund). Examples:

  • talk him into going
  • talk her into buying it
  • talk them into staying

You can never say "talk him into go" or "talk her into buy it." The -ing form is mandatory.
The Core Idea — Resistance Then Agreement

The most important thing to understand is this: there is always some resistance at the beginning.

The person you are talking to:

  • didn't want to do it, OR
  • was unsure, OR
  • had doubts or hesitation

Then, after you talked to them — used reasons, explanations, flattery, emotion, logic, or even pressure — they changed their mind and agreed.

This is what makes this idiom different from simply "asking." When you ask someone to do something, you don't know if they'll say yes. But when you talk someone into something, the result is already known — they said yes. The persuasion worked.
Examples in Real Life

1. A friend convincing another friend:

"I didn't want to go to the party, but Sarah talked me into it."

2. A salesperson:

"The car salesman talked us into buying the more expensive model."

(You went to buy a cheaper car, but after the conversation, you left with the expensive one.)

3. Family situation:

"My kids talked me into getting a dog."

(You were not planning to get a dog. Your kids kept asking and explaining and convincing — and eventually you agreed.)

4. Workplace:

"She talked her manager into giving her an extra week of vacation."

(The manager wasn't going to give it. She made arguments. The manager agreed.)
The Feeling/Tone of This Idiom

This idiom can carry different feelings depending on the situation:

Neutral or Positive tone — when the result was actually good:

"He talked me into trying sushi, and I loved it!"

Here, you're glad someone convinced you.

Slightly negative tone — when you feel manipulated or regret the decision:

"She talked me into lending her money, and she never paid me back."

Here, you feel like you were pushed into something you shouldn't have done.

So the idiom itself is neutral in meaning but the context gives it a positive or negative color.
The Opposite: "Talk Someone Out of Something"

The exact opposite idiom is "talk someone out of something," which means to persuade someone NOT to do something they were already planning to do.

  • Talk into = convince someone to DO something
  • Talk out of = convince someone NOT to do something

Examples of the opposite:

"He was going to quit his job, but his wife talked him out of it."
"I was about to buy that expensive jacket, but my friend talked me out of it."

Learning both together makes each one clearer.
Related Expressions That Mean Similar Things

These idioms and phrases carry a similar meaning and are useful to know:

  • Convince someone to do something — the most direct equivalent, but more formal
  • Persuade someone to do something — same idea, slightly formal
  • Win someone over — to gradually bring someone to your side
  • Bring someone around — to change someone's opinion over time
  • Twist someone's arm — to pressure someone heavily into doing something (more forceful than "talk into")
  • Get someone to do something — casual and broad, doesn't emphasize the verbal effort

Among all of these, "talk someone into something" specifically emphasizes that it was done through talking and verbal persuasion. The "talking" is the key tool used.
How It Feels to Use This Idiom Naturally

This is a very common, everyday English idiom. Native speakers use it in casual conversation all the time. It sounds completely natural in:

  • Spoken conversation — "How did you end up going?" / "Oh, my brother talked me into it."
  • Storytelling — "So she talked the whole team into staying late."
  • Writing — articles, stories, emails — it fits everywhere

It is not rude, not slang, and not too formal. It's perfectly balanced for all situations.
One Common Mistake to Avoid

Learners sometimes say:

❌ "She talked me into to go."
❌ "He talked her into do it."

Always remember: after "into," you need the -ing form:

✅ "She talked me into going."
✅ "He talked her into doing it."
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

"Talk someone into something" = to use words and arguments to convince a person to do something they originally didn't plan or want to do — and succeed.

The person resists → you use words → they agree. That's the whole story.
15731: This idiom describes someone who talks excessively — so much, so persistently, and for so long that it becomes exhausting just to be around them. If you say someone "could talk the hind legs off a donkey," you mean they are an unstoppable, long-winded talker who simply cannot stop once they start.

To really understand this idiom, picture the literal image for a moment.

A donkey is a stubborn, tough, hard-working animal. Its hind legs — the two back legs — are what keep it standing upright and moving. Now imagine someone talking so relentlessly and with such endurance that their non-stop words could somehow wear down those legs, causing them to literally fall off, leaving the donkey collapsed on the ground.

Of course, talking cannot actually remove a donkey's legs. That is exactly the point. The idiom uses wild exaggeration — a literary device called hyperbole — to show just how extreme the person's talking is. The idea is: if you could talk the legs off a tough, strong animal, your talking must be truly extraordinary in its persistence and force.
Why a Donkey? Why the Hind Legs?

The choice of a donkey is very deliberate. Donkeys are famous in folk culture for being stubborn and difficult to move. They dig their hooves in and refuse to budge. So if someone's talking can overpower even a notoriously stubborn creature, that tells you something powerful about the sheer relentlessness of their speech.

The hind legs are singled out because they are the animal's main source of standing power and forward movement. Without its hind legs, a donkey collapses completely — it cannot stand, it cannot escape. The image is of talk so overwhelming that even the most resistant, sturdy creature would be brought crashing down.

This is a very old British idiom, with printed records dating back to at least 1808, making it over two hundred years old. Despite its age, it has stayed in common, natural use in British and Australian English to this day.

In its early life, the expression existed in variations using other animals — "talk the hind leg off a horse" and "talk the hind leg off a dog" were both used. Over time, the donkey became the animal most associated with the idiom, likely because of the donkey's strong cultural image as a stubborn, unyielding creature — making the exaggeration feel even more extreme.

This idiom is generally not a compliment, but it is rarely a harsh insult either. It is most often used in a humorous, slightly exasperated, or even affectionate way — the kind of thing you might say about a chatty friend or a well-loved family member with a smile and a shake of the head.

Importantly, the idiom says nothing about the quality of what a person says. They are not necessarily boring, unintelligent, or dishonest. They may even be fascinating! The idiom is purely about quantity and persistence — the person simply will not stop talking.

This idiom belongs firmly to British English and Australian English. If you are learning or living in an American English environment, you will hear it rarely. The American equivalent for the same idea is usually "talk someone's ear off" — different image, same meaning.

If you read British novels, watch British or Australian TV programmes, or spend time speaking with people from those regions, you are very likely to come across this expression.
How to Use It — Examples in Context

Here are several natural examples across different situations:

"My grandfather could talk the hind legs off a donkey — I once sat with him for two hours and managed to say about four words."

"Don't ask her about her holiday unless you have the whole afternoon free. She'll talk the hind legs off a donkey."

"He's a wonderful man, but he talks the hind legs off a donkey. You'll need to invent an excuse to leave."

"I only called to confirm the time of the meeting, and he talked the hind legs off a donkey before I could say goodbye."

You can even use it jokingly about yourself: "Sorry, I'm probably talking the hind legs off a donkey here!" — which shows self-awareness about your own talkativeness, and usually gets a laugh.

It does not mean the person is stupid, boring, or a liar. It does not mean their ideas lack value. A brilliant professor, a witty comedian, or a deeply knowledgeable expert can all "talk the hind legs off a donkey." The idiom focuses entirely on the amount and endurance of the talking — not on what is being said.

You will see both forms used — "hind leg" (singular) and "hind legs" (plural). Both are perfectly correct. Neither is more formal or more proper than the other. The plural form is slightly more common in everyday modern usage, but you will encounter both without any difference in meaning.

If someone "talks the hind legs off a donkey," they are an extreme, unstoppable talker — someone who goes on and on with great energy and persistence until everyone around them is thoroughly worn out. It is a colourful, centuries-old British expression that uses comic exaggeration to describe one very simple human truth: some people simply cannot stop talking.
15732:
To talk up something or someone means to speak about them in a very positive, enthusiastic way in order to make others think highly of them. When you talk something up, you are actively promoting it, praising it, or building excitement around it — often with the goal of influencing how others feel about it.

Think of it this way: you are using your words to lift something in other people's eyes. You are making it sound great, impressive, or worth paying attention to.

"Talk up" has a few distinct uses.

Meaning 1: To Praise or Promote Something / Someone

This is by far the most common and important meaning.

When you talk up something, you say good things about it to make others interested in it, excited about it, or convinced that it is valuable.

Examples:

  • "The travel agent talked up the hotel so much that we were convinced to book it."
    → The agent praised the hotel enthusiastically to persuade the customers.
  • "He has been talking up his new business idea to every investor he meets."
    → He keeps promoting and praising his idea to attract investors.
  • "The coach talked up his players before the match to boost their confidence."
    → The coach said great things about his players to build excitement and morale.
  • "The film studio talked up the movie months before its release."
    → The studio hyped the movie and created buzz around it.

An important nuance here: "Talk up" can be genuine or slightly exaggerated. Sometimes a person talks something up honestly because they truly believe in it. But sometimes they talk it up strategically — meaning they may be overselling it a little, making it sound better than it really is.

For example:

  • "The salesperson talked up the car so much, but when we actually drove it, we were disappointed."
    → Here, the talking up was exaggerated and not fully honest.

This is why "talk up" can carry a mild sense of spin or marketing language in some contexts. The core meaning is still positive promotion, but depending on the situation, it can hint at a little exaggeration.

Meaning 2: To Speak to Someone Confidently and Directly

This meaning is less common but worth knowing.

To talk up to someone can mean to speak to a person of higher authority or status in a direct, confident, even bold way — without being overly timid or submissive.

Example:

  • "Don't be afraid to talk up to your manager if you think the decision is wrong."
    → Speak directly and confidently; don't stay silent out of fear.

This usage is relatively informal and less frequently used than the first meaning.

Meaning 3: To Speak More Loudly (Informal, Mainly British)

In informal British English, "talk up" (or more commonly "speak up") can sometimes mean to raise your voice so others can hear you better.

Example:

  • "Could you talk up a bit? The people at the back can't hear you."
    → Please speak louder.

This meaning is minor and context-specific. If you are in a conversation and someone says "talk up," they almost certainly mean Meaning 1 — promotion and praise.

"Talk up" is a phrasal verb — that means it is a verb ("talk") combined with a particle ("up") to create a new, specific meaning. The word "up" here does not literally mean an upward direction. Instead, it adds the idea of elevating or boosting something.

The grammar pattern:

You can structure it in two ways, and both are correct:

  1. Talk up + object → "She talked up the new product."
  2. Talk + object + up → "She talked the new product up."

Both sentences mean exactly the same thing.

However, if you use a pronoun (like it, him, her, them), you must place it in the middle:

  • ✅ "She talked it up." (correct)
  • ❌ "She talked up it." (incorrect)

More examples of this grammar:

  • "The journalist talked up the new policy." / "The journalist talked the new policy up."
  • "They talked him up to the board of directors." (They praised him to the board.)
  • "Stop talking it up — it's not that great."

"Talk up" is an informal to semi-formal expression. You can use it in everyday conversation, in news articles, in business contexts, and in sports commentary. It is widely used in English-speaking countries, especially in British, American, and Australian English.

It is not rude or inappropriate in any way. It is simply natural, common English.
Real-World Contexts Where You'll See It

In business and finance:

  • "The CEO talked up the company's growth potential in an interview with investors."
  • "Analysts have been talking up the stock for months."

In politics:

  • "The minister talked up the new infrastructure project during her speech."

In sports:

  • "The captain talked up his team's chances before the final."

In everyday life:

  • "My friend talked up that restaurant so much that I had to try it."
  • "He always talks up his cooking, but it's just average."

In entertainment:

  • "The director spent months talking up the film at festivals before its release."

It is worth being clear about what "talk up" does not mean, so you do not confuse it with similar phrases:

  • It does not mean to have a conversation with someone. ("I talked up my friend" does not mean "I had a chat with my friend." It means "I praised my friend to others.")
  • It does not mean to shout at someone or speak in an aggressive way. It is about positive promotion, not aggression.
  • It does not mean to exaggerate negatively. If someone is saying bad things to influence others, that is talking down something, not talking it up.
Related Phrases That Are Good to Know

Understanding these similar phrases will give you a fuller picture:

Talk down — the opposite of talk up. To minimize, criticize, or make something sound less impressive. Also, to talk to someone in a condescending way (as if they are less intelligent).
"He always talks down his rivals."

Hype up — very similar to "talk up," but stronger. It implies heavy, sometimes excessive promotion.
"The media hyped up the new phone before launch."

Big up — informal (especially British slang) for praising and showing appreciation for someone.
"Big up to everyone who helped organize the event."

Talk someone into something — to persuade someone to do something through conversation.
"She talked me into trying the new restaurant." (Different from talking it up — here, persuasion leads to an action.)

Here is a clean summary without a table:

"Talk up" most commonly means to speak positively and enthusiastically about something or someone in order to promote it, build excitement around it, or make others see it in a favorable light. It can be genuine praise or a slightly exaggerated, strategic form of promotion. Less commonly, it means to speak boldly to someone of authority, or to speak more loudly. It is a natural, informal-to-semi-formal phrasal verb used across everyday life, business, sports, politics, and media.
One Final Example to Tie It All Together

Imagine a friend opens a small bakery. She asks you to help spread the word. You go to your workplace, your family gatherings, and your social circle and you say things like: "This bakery is incredible — the croissants melt in your mouth, the coffee is perfect, and the prices are very reasonable. You absolutely have to visit."

You are talking up her bakery. You are using your words to make others see it positively, to build interest, and to encourage them to visit. That is "talk up" in its purest, most common form.
15733:
Talkative describes a person who talks a lot — noticeably more than most people do. A talkative person enjoys conversation, starts it easily, keeps it going, and tends to speak at length. They rarely sit in silence when there's someone around to talk to.

Think of someone who can fill a quiet room just by being in it, who always has something to say, and who often speaks more than others in a group. That person is talkative.

Talkative doesn't mean the person never stops talking or that they're annoying about it. It simply means they're on the higher end of the talking scale — more than average, but not necessarily too much.

Imagine a scale like this:

Silent → Quiet → Average → Talkative → Excessively talkative

Talkative sits comfortably in the upper-middle. It's the person who keeps the conversation alive, not the one who won't let others speak.

This is where it gets interesting. Talkative is mostly neutral, but its tone shifts depending on context.

  • Positive context: "She's so talkative — I never feel awkward around her." Here, it means she's warm, engaging, and easy to be with.
  • Neutral context: "He's just naturally talkative — that's how he is." A simple description, no judgment.
  • Mildly negative context: "She was so talkative that I couldn't get a word in." Here, it leans toward too much talking.

So the word itself isn't an insult, but it can carry a gentle complaint depending on how it's used. It's one of those words where tone and context do a lot of the work.

Talkative can describe both a lasting personality trait and a temporary mood or state.

  • Trait: "My aunt is a very talkative person." — She's always been this way; it's part of who she is.
  • Temporary: "He was unusually talkative today." — Something made him open up more than usual; maybe he was excited or nervous.

This flexibility is worth remembering. When you say "she's talkative," it usually means it's her nature. When you say "she seems talkative tonight," it suggests it's out of the ordinary for her.
Words Similar to Talkative (and How They Differ)

Understanding the words around "talkative" will sharpen your sense of exactly what it means.

Chatty — Very similar to talkative, but more informal and warmer in feel. A chatty person makes friendly, light conversation. "She's so chatty over text!" You'd use chatty in casual settings; it rarely feels like a complaint.

Loquacious — This is a formal, elevated word for someone who talks a great deal — often at impressive length and fluency. It's talkative turned up a notch, and used in more formal or literary writing. "The professor was loquacious but always fascinating."

Garrulous — This one leans negative. A garrulous person talks too much, often about unimportant things, and others might find it tiresome. "The garrulous old man told the same stories three times." If talkative is neutral, garrulous is talkative with a complaint attached.

Verbose — Mainly used for writing or speech that uses far more words than needed. "His verbose emails took ten minutes to read." It's about excess, not personality.

Voluble — Means speaking with great ease and fluency, often rapidly and at length. It has a slightly impressive quality to it. Less commonly used in everyday conversation.

Communicative — This just means willing to share information and talk openly. It's more neutral and broader — it doesn't suggest talking a lot, just that the person doesn't hold back.

If talkative is one end, these are the other:

  • Quiet / Silent — The most everyday opposites.
  • Reserved — The person keeps to themselves and doesn't open up easily.
  • Reticent — Unwilling or hesitant to speak, especially about personal things. "He was reticent about his past."
  • Taciturn — Habitually saying very little; a person of few words. This is the precise opposite of talkative. "She gave taciturn, one-word answers."
  • Tight-lipped — Deliberately not saying much, often because of caution or secrecy.

Here are sentences showing how talkative works in real use:

  1. My little cousin is incredibly talkative — she started telling me about her day before I'd even sat down.
  2. He's usually quiet, but he gets talkative when the topic turns to football.
  3. The new employee was friendly and talkative, which helped ease the tension in the office.
  4. She wasn't feeling well and was much less talkative than normal.
  5. Don't ask him about his trip unless you have an hour to spare — he's very talkative about travel.
  6. The talkative child kept asking questions throughout the entire museum tour.
  7. Nervousness makes some people go silent; it makes others go talkative.

Talkative = someone who talks a lot and readily, as a natural part of who they are or how they're feeling in a moment — described in a neutral, sometimes gently positive, sometimes mildly critical way depending on context.
15734:
When someone says something is "a tall order," they mean it is a very difficult, demanding, or challenging task or request — something that requires a lot of effort, skill, time, or resources to accomplish.

It does not necessarily mean something is completely impossible. It simply means it is unusually hard — the kind of thing that makes you think, "Wow, that won't be easy."

Think of it like being asked to carry a very tall, heavy stack of boxes. It's not impossible, but it's a lot to handle.
A Simple Everyday Example

Imagine your boss says:

"I need you to write a 50-page report by tomorrow morning."

You might reply:

"That's a tall order, but I'll do my best."

You're saying: "That's a lot to ask and it will be really hard, but I'll try."
Where It Comes From (The Origin)

The idiom comes from old American business language, likely from the 19th century.

In business, an "order" is a request to buy or supply goods — like a customer ordering 10,000 units of a product from a factory. If someone placed an extremely large or difficult-to-fill order, it was called a "tall order" — because "tall" in older American slang meant large, bold, or excessive.

Over time, the phrase left the business world and entered everyday language. Now it's used for any situation — not just business — where something is very hard to do or fulfill.

This same use of "tall" to mean big/excessive/demanding also appears in related expressions:

  • "Tall tale" — an exaggerated, hard-to-believe story
  • "Tall talk" — boastful or overblown speech

So the core idea of "tall" = a lot / too much / very demanding has been consistent across English for a long time.
How to Use It — The Structure

The idiom is most commonly used in a few natural patterns:

1. "That's a tall order."
Used to respond when someone asks for something very difficult.

"Can you learn Spanish in two weeks?"
"That's a tall order, but I'll try."

2. "It's a tall order to..."
Used to describe a difficult task or challenge.

"It's a tall order to please everyone at the same time."

3. "Asking someone to do something is a tall order."
Used to point out that the request placed on someone is very demanding.

"Asking a first-year student to teach the class is a tall order."

4. "A tall order, but not impossible."
A common pattern used to acknowledge difficulty while expressing confidence.

"Finishing the construction in three months is a tall order, but not impossible."
Formal or Informal?

Both. This is one of the most versatile idioms in English.

  • You'll hear it in casual conversation between friends.
  • You'll read it in newspapers, business reports, and political commentary.
  • You'll hear it in professional meetings and formal speeches.

It is never rude, offensive, or out of place. It suits almost any context.
The Tone It Carries

"A tall order" usually carries a respectful or realistic tone. When you call something a tall order, you are:

  • Acknowledging the difficulty — you're not dismissing the challenge.
  • Not necessarily complaining — it's a neutral observation, not a refusal.
  • Sometimes expressing admiration — recognizing that achieving it would be impressive.

For example:

"Winning three Olympic gold medals in one Games is a tall order — only a handful of athletes in history have done it."

Here, calling it a tall order adds weight and respect to the achievement.
Real-Life Contexts Where You'll Hear It

• In politics: "Winning the election after that scandal will be a tall order for the party."
  • In sports: "Coming back from 3–0 down is a tall order, but this team has done it before."
  • In education: "Expecting students to master calculus in a month is a tall order."
  • At work: "Launching the product by Friday? That's a tall order given the team's current workload."
  • In everyday life: "Cooking a five-course meal for 30 people by yourself is a tall order."
What It Is NOT Saying

Be careful about these common misunderstandings:

  • It does not mean something is tall in height. It has nothing to do with physical height.
  • It does not mean something is impossible. It means very difficult, which is different.
  • It does not imply refusal. You can call something a tall order and still agree to do it.
Similar Expressions (Same or Close Meaning)

These idioms share a similar meaning and are good to know alongside "a tall order":

  • "A big ask" — very commonly used in British English; means requesting something very demanding. "It's a big ask, but can you cover my shift?"
  • "No small feat" — used to say that something is an impressive and difficult achievement. "Finishing the race was no small feat."
  • "Easier said than done" — means something sounds simple but is actually hard to do.
  • "A hard row to hoe" — an older, more rural idiom meaning a difficult task or situation ahead.
Opposite Expressions

When something is easy (the opposite of a tall order), people use:

  • "A piece of cake" — very easy.
  • "A walk in the park" — effortless.
  • "A cinch" — simple and easy.
  • "Child's play" — so easy that even a child could do it.
One-Line Summary to Remember It Forever

"A tall order" = a task or request that is very difficult and demands a great deal of effort — challenging, but not always impossible.

Whenever someone asks for something unusually hard — something that makes you pause and think, "That's a LOT" — you can say: "That's a tall order."
15735: Tallow is a hard, solid fat made from animals — specifically cattle or sheep. It is not the raw fat you see on a piece of meat. It is what you get after that raw fat has been slowly melted down, cleaned, and purified. The result is a smooth, firm, whitish or pale yellowish substance, somewhat like a wax block, that is solid at room temperature but melts easily when heated.
What it comes from

Tallow comes from the fatty tissue of cows (called beef tallow) or sheep (called mutton tallow). The specific raw fat used is usually taken from around the kidneys and internal organs, where it is the hardest and purest. This raw form of hard animal fat — before it is processed — is called suet. When suet is slowly heated to separate the pure fat from connective tissue, blood, and other impurities, the resulting purified fat is tallow. So: suet is the raw material; tallow is the finished, clean product.

Don't confuse tallow with lard, which is the same kind of rendered fat — but from pigs, not cattle or sheep.
What it looks, feels, and smells like

• Appearance: Solid, opaque, usually white to pale cream or yellow.
  • Texture: Waxy, firm, and dense — somewhat like a bar of unscented soap or a thick candle.
  • Smell: Mild, faintly meaty or fatty smell. High-quality, well-rendered tallow is nearly odourless.
  • Behaviour with heat: Melts smoothly into a clear, golden liquid when warmed. Solidifies again as it cools.
What makes tallow special or useful

Tallow has two key properties that have made it valuable across human history:

  1. It is very stable: Because it is high in saturated fat, tallow does not go rancid (spoil) quickly. It can be stored for a long time without refrigeration.
  2. It has a high smoke point: When used for cooking, it can be heated to high temperatures without burning, making it excellent for frying and searing.
How tallow has been used (and still is)
Tallow has served humanity in an enormous range of roles:
In the kitchen:

Tallow was one of the most common cooking fats before vegetable oils became widespread. It was used for deep frying, roasting, and pan-cooking. Many people still cook with beef tallow today for its rich flavour and high heat stability. For decades, fast food chains (including McDonald's) famously fried their potatoes in beef tallow — widely credited for a superior flavour.
For candles:

Before electricity, tallow candles were the everyday candles of ordinary people. Beeswax candles existed too, but were expensive. Tallow candles were cheap and widely available because slaughtered cattle and sheep were already being used for meat. They burned well, though they had a faint animal smell.
For soap:

Tallow is a core ingredient in traditional soap-making. When tallow is mixed with an alkali (like lye), a chemical reaction occurs that creates soap. Many commercial soaps still contain tallow-derived ingredients today, though it may not say "tallow" on the label directly.
As a lubricant:

Before modern synthetic lubricants, tallow was smeared on axles, hinges, gears, ropes, and machinery to reduce friction. It was practical, affordable, and widely available. Sailors rubbed it on ropes and wooden hulls. Blacksmiths used it on tools and leather.
For waterproofing:
Tallow was rubbed onto leather shoes, boots, saddles, and ropes to make them water-resistant and to prevent cracking and drying out.
In skincare:

Tallow has seen a renewed interest in natural skincare. When applied to skin, it absorbs easily because its fat composition is structurally similar to the fats found in human skin. It is used in balms, moisturisers, and salves, particularly for dry or irritated skin.
As a modern biofuel:
Tallow is used in the production of biodiesel — a type of fuel derived from fats and oils — and is part of the supply chain for certain industrial processes.
A quick sense of its place in the larger world

Think of tallow as one of humanity's oldest multi-purpose materials. For most of human history — before petroleum, before vegetable oils at scale, before synthetic chemicals — tallow was what people reached for when they needed something to cook in, burn for light, lubricate with, or clean themselves with. It is a byproduct of animal agriculture, so it has always been naturally available wherever livestock were raised. Even today, it remains useful, practical, and valued by people who prefer natural, traditional, or animal-based products.
In a sentence

If someone says "they rendered tallow from the beef suet", it means: they slowly melted down the hard raw fat from the cattle, separated out the impurities, and collected the clean, solid fat that was left — which is tallow.
15736: The verb tally has two distinct meanings. Both are common, and both are worth understanding fully.
Meaning 1: To count something, keeping a running total

When you tally something, you count it carefully — usually item by item — and keep track of the growing total as you go. The key idea is progressive counting: you're not just glancing at a pile and estimating; you're recording each item as you count it, building up a record.

A teacher who wants to know how many students prefer option A versus option B might tally the raised hands — making a mark for each one, so the count is tracked as it happens. A shop owner who tallies up the day's sales goes through each transaction one by one and adds the amounts together.

The phrase "tally up" is extremely common and means exactly this — to add things up to get a final total. You'll hear it constantly:

  • "Can you tally up the scores?"
  • "She spent an hour tallying up the expenses."
  • "Let's tally up how many people confirmed attendance."

You'll also encounter this meaning in sports, where it has a slightly specific use: to tally points, goals, or runs means to have scored or accumulated them. "He tallied 30 points in the match" means he scored and accumulated 30 points over the course of the game. The underlying idea is the same — a count is being built up.

The feeling that tally carries in this sense is one of methodical tracking. It suggests that someone is carefully keeping a record, not just doing a rough count. When someone tallies something, they're being systematic.
Meaning 2: To match or be consistent with something

This is the second — and arguably equally important — meaning of tally as a verb. When two things tally, they agree with each other. They are consistent, they correspond, they line up. When two things don't tally, there is a contradiction or a discrepancy between them.

This meaning almost always appears with the word "with": something tallies with something else.

  • "His account of the incident doesn't tally with what the witness described."
    → His story and the witness's story contradict each other; they don't match.
  • "The number of votes cast should tally with the number of voters who signed in."
    → The two numbers should be consistent and equal.
  • "Her fingerprints tallied with those found at the crime scene."
    → They matched precisely.
  • "The delivery receipt doesn't tally with what was actually shipped."
    → There's a discrepancy between what the receipt says and what was actually sent.

Notice something important about this meaning: tally implies a specific, precise kind of matching — not vague resemblance or general similarity, but exact correspondence when two things are carefully compared. It's the word you use when you're verifying whether two things agree. It carries the sense of a check or a comparison being performed.

This is why you'll often find this meaning in contexts involving investigations, audits, accounts, testimonies, and data:

  • "The post-match statistics didn't tally with what the coach had described."
  • "Investigators found that the alibi failed to tally with the CCTV footage."
  • "The two financial reports tally — there are no discrepancies."

You can also use tally in this sense without "with", when you're saying that multiple things are mutually consistent with each other: "The two accounts tally" simply means they agree with each other.
How the two meanings are connected

The link between "counting" and "matching" is intuitive once you think about it.

Imagine two people counting the same batch of ballots independently. When they finish, they compare their numbers. If both counted 547 — if the numbers agree — their tallies have tallied. The idea of matching or agreement grew directly out of the act of counting: two counts tally when they arrive at the same result.

So both meanings share a core concept: correspondence and exactness. Whether you're keeping a careful running count, or checking whether two figures agree, tally is always about precision and careful tracking.
How to tell which meaning is being used

Counting sense: Tally has a direct object — something being counted or added up.

  • "Tally the votes." / "She tallied up the costs."

Matching sense: Tally is followed by "with," or it describes two things being compared.

  • "It doesn't tally with the facts." / "The two stories tally."
Common contexts where you'll encounter this word

• Elections: "Officials tallied the ballots through the night." (counting)
  • Finance: "The expenses tallied up to more than expected." (counting); "The figures in the two reports don't tally." (matching)
  • Sports: "She tallied 15 goals this season." (scored/accumulated)
  • Law and investigations: "His testimony didn't tally with the evidence." (matching)
  • Everyday life: "Can you tally up how many are coming for dinner?" (counting)

To tally means either (1) to count something carefully, keeping a running total — often used with up — or (2) to match or agree with something, used when comparing two things for consistency, almost always with with. The two senses are connected by the same underlying idea: exactness and careful correspondence. The first is about building a precise count; the second is about whether two things, when checked against each other, come to the same result.
15737:
A talon is a sharp, curved, hook-like claw found on the foot of a bird of prey — meaning a hunting bird like an eagle, hawk, owl, falcon, osprey, or vulture.

When you picture an eagle's foot, those thick, pointed, deeply curved claws gripping a branch or snatching a fish from a river — those are talons.
What Exactly Does a Talon Look Like?

A talon is not a flat or gentle curve. It is:

  • Thick and powerful at the base
  • Sharply curved like a fishhook
  • Pointed to a fine tip
  • Made of keratin — the same tough material as your fingernails, only far denser and harder

A bird of prey typically has four talons on each foot — three pointing forward and one pointing backward (called the hallux). This arrangement lets the bird lock its grip around prey with tremendous force.

Talons are not just for perching. They are active, deadly hunting tools:

  • A hunting bird dives at high speed and drives its talons into prey — piercing the body and often killing the animal on contact through sheer force and puncture.
  • Talons are used to grip and carry prey through the air, sometimes over long distances.
  • They are used for defense against other animals or rival birds.
  • An osprey, for example, has special spiny pads on its feet to help its talons hold slippery fish.

The grip strength of talons is extraordinary. A bald eagle's talons can exert a gripping pressure many times stronger than an average human hand.
Talon vs. Claw — An Important Distinction

This is where many learners get confused, so let's be precise:

All talons are claws, but not all claws are talons.

The word talon is specifically and correctly used only for birds of prey. Other animals have claws — cats have claws, bears have claws, chickens have claws — but none of those are called talons. A chicken scratches with its claws. An eagle hunts with its talons.

The distinction is both about the type of animal (a predatory bird) and the nature of the claw (built for seizing, piercing, and gripping live prey). Using "talon" for a cat or a lizard would be technically incorrect, even though the structure looks similar.

In everyday writing and speech, talon is also used figuratively to describe anything that grips, clutches, or threatens in a sharp and predatory way — usually to suggest danger, control, or menace.

For example:

  • "She felt the talon of fear grip her chest."
  • "The corrupt official kept the whole city in his talons."
  • "He escaped the talons of debt only after years of struggle."

In these cases, the word is not describing a literal bird's claw — it's borrowing the imagery of something sharp, inescapable, and predatory.
Other Specific Uses of the Word

While the bird's claw is by far the most common meaning, talon appears in a few other specific contexts:

1. In card games:
The talon refers to the pile of undealt cards that remains after the initial deal — essentially the leftover deck that players may draw from. This usage is common in older European card games.

2. In architecture:
A talon is a specific type of decorative molding (a shaped edge or trim) that has an S-shaped curve — convex on top and concave on the bottom. This is a very specialized term used by architects and builders.

3. In heraldry (the design of coats of arms):
In heraldic art, the claws of any creature — not just birds of prey — depicted on a shield or crest may be called talons.

4. In dentistry:
A talon cusp is a rare anatomical variation where an extra, pointed cusp (a small projection) grows on the back surface of a tooth, resembling a talon in shape.
A talon is the powerful, sharply curved claw of a hunting bird — and by extension, anything that grips, clutches, or threatens with predatory force.
15738:
The word tame means lacking wildness. Everything this word does — in every context — comes down to that. Something tame has had its wildness removed, controlled, or simply never had any to begin with.

Its opposite is always wild. Keep that contrast in mind and the word becomes very easy to use.

A tame animal is one that does not behave wildly around humans. It doesn't attack, doesn't flee in fear, and accepts human presence, touch, or commands calmly.

A tame animal:

  • Lets you approach it without running away
  • Doesn't attack out of fear or aggression
  • Can be handled, fed by hand, or kept near people safely

Examples:

  • "The deer was so tame it walked right up to us and ate from our hands."
  • "After weeks of gentle handling, the parrot became completely tame."
  • "The farmer kept a tame crow that would sit on his shoulder."

Important: A tame animal is not necessarily a loving pet. It simply means the animal has lost its wild, dangerous edge around people. A wolf raised by humans from birth can be tame. A lion trained to accept handlers can be tame. The key idea is: safe and calm around humans, not wild.

The contrast in one sentence: A wild bear will charge at you or run. A tame bear has been raised around people and will do neither.
Meaning 2: A Person Who Is Too Easy to Control

When used to describe a person, "tame" is almost always slightly critical. It means someone who is too obedient, too submissive, or lacking in boldness and independent spirit. They never push back, never surprise you, and are very easy to control or predict.

Examples:

  • "We needed a strong leader, but he was far too tame — he just went along with whatever others said."
  • "She used to be fierce and outspoken, but years in that job made her tame."

Think of it this way: if a wild animal has spirit and force, and a tame animal has had that spirit calmed into submission — then calling a person tame suggests their inner strength or courage has been similarly flattened. It can sometimes sound like an insult because it implies the person has been "domesticated" — stripped of their edge.
Meaning 3: Events and Situations That Lack Excitement

This is one of the most common everyday uses. When a situation or event is described as tame, it means it was milder and less intense than expected. Nothing dramatic happened. There was no real danger, thrill, confrontation, or surprise.

Examples:

  • "After all the warnings, the protest turned out to be completely tame — people just marched quietly and went home."
  • "The party was pretty tame; everyone just sat around and talked."
  • "Compared to last year's championship, this year's final was tame."

The word often carries a hint of disappointment here. You expected something bold or intense, and instead got something safe and forgettable. It doesn't always mean the speaker is unhappy — sometimes "tame" is neutral, as in "it was a tame evening" meaning simply a quiet, uneventful one. But the slight shade of letdown is very common.
Meaning 4: Content or Creative Work That Lacks Edge

When applied to jokes, films, writing, criticism, or performances, tame means the content is too soft, too safe, and lacking real sharpness or impact. It held back when it should have been bold.

Examples:

  • "That horror movie was tame — not a single scary moment."
  • "His jokes were too tame for that crowd; no one laughed."
  • "Her review of the book was surprisingly tame; she never really said anything daring."
  • "For an action thriller, the fight scenes felt disappointingly tame."

Here, "tame" suggests the work played it safe. A tame joke doesn't push any buttons. A tame villain in a movie isn't truly menacing. A tame piece of criticism avoids saying anything too uncomfortable. The word tells you that something which should have had force or edge simply didn't.
The Single Thread Running Through Every Use

Context"Wild" would mean"Tame" means

In every situation, "tame" signals the absence of something intense:

  • A tame animal is missing its dangerous, unpredictable wildness.
  • A tame person is missing their bold, independent spirit.
  • A tame event is missing its excitement and drama.
  • A tame piece of content is missing its sharpness and edge.

Wherever you encounter the word, ask yourself: "Wild compared to what?" — and whatever that answer is, "tame" is telling you it's falling short of it.

The word works in comparisons and is easy to intensify:

  • "That was a bit tame." → Slightly underwhelming
  • "That was pretty tame." → Noticeably mild
  • "That was completely tame." → No edge whatsoever
  • "That was tamer than I expected." → It had some energy, just not enough
  • "The second film was even tamer than the first." → Getting progressively milder

Knowing similar words helps you feel the exact weight of "tame":

  • For animals: docile, domesticated, gentle, obedient
  • For people: meek, submissive, compliant, timid
  • For events/content: dull, bland, mild, uninspiring, flat, uneventful, safe

"Tame" often sits somewhere between completely harmless and disappointingly average. It's not the worst thing you can call something — but it's rarely a compliment.
One Final Tip for Using It Correctly

"Tame" almost always implies a contrast — either with something wilder that came before, or with something wilder that was expected. When someone says "the movie was tame," they're measuring it against what a bold, intense version of that movie could have been. When they say "the animal is tame," they're measuring it against how it would behave in the wild. Always look for that invisible comparison — that's where the true meaning lives.
15739:
"To tame" means to bring something wild, powerful, or uncontrolled under your control — to make it calm, manageable, and no longer a threat or a problem.

The key idea hiding inside this word is a before and after. Before taming, something is free, fierce, unpredictable, or overwhelming. After taming, it is obedient, gentle, or at least no longer out of control. Something has been changed from its wild or chaotic state into something more manageable.
Meaning 1: Making a Wild Animal Gentle

This is the most classic use of the word. A wild animal — say, a lion, a wolf, or a falcon — lives entirely on its own terms. It fears humans, follows its instincts, and cannot be controlled. When you tame it, you slowly earn its trust and teach it to accept human presence and commands. It stops being dangerous around you. It becomes cooperative.

Examples:

  • "It took the trainer years to tame the wild horse."
  • "The villagers were amazed that she had tamed the wolf."

Notice that taming an animal is not the same as training it. Training teaches specific skills and tricks. Taming changes the animal's fundamental relationship with humans — it removes the fear and aggression that make the animal wild in the first place. You tame first, then train. A lion in a circus has been both tamed (it tolerates and trusts humans) and trained (it has learned specific behaviors).

Also notice that taming is a gradual process, not a single event. It takes patience, repeated effort, and time. This idea of slow, persistent effort is embedded in the word.
Meaning 2: Bringing a Powerful Force Under Control

"Tame" is very commonly used for powerful forces of nature — things that are wild not because they are animals, but because they are enormous, chaotic, and destructive.

Examples:

  • "Engineers built dams to tame the river." (The river used to flood and destroy villages. Now it is controlled.)
  • "Firefighters worked through the night to tame the wildfire."
  • "Early settlers struggled to tame the wilderness."

In these cases, nobody is making friends with the river or the fire. Instead, they are simply bringing it under control — reducing its power to harm or disrupt. The force still exists, but it no longer runs free and does whatever it wants.
Meaning 3: Reducing Something Intense or Extreme

Here, "tame" moves fully into abstract territory. It means to reduce the intensity, extremity, or sharpness of something — to soften it, calm it down, or make it less powerful than it was.

Examples:

  • "The government took steps to tame inflation." (Prices were rising wildly and uncontrollably. The measures brought that under control.)
  • "She tried to tame her anger before responding to him."
  • "The editor asked the writer to tame some of the more aggressive language in the article."
  • "He needed to tame his ambitions and be more realistic."

In each of these, something was excessive, intense, or out of control — and taming it means pulling it back, reducing it to a manageable level. It doesn't disappear entirely; it is simply no longer running wild.
Meaning 4: Controlling or Subduing a Person

When used on a person, "to tame someone" means to bring a difficult, rebellious, fierce, or unruly person under control — to break their resistance, cool their fierceness, or make them more obedient and cooperative.

Examples:

  • "Nobody in the school could tame that troublesome student — until she arrived."
  • "He was a wild and reckless young man. Life eventually tamed him."

This usage is interesting because it often carries a slightly complex tone. Sometimes it is admiring — the person has matured or calmed down. Other times it can feel a little sad, as if something lively or spirited about them has been suppressed or lost. Context decides which feeling the word carries.
The Deeper Feeling of the Word

"Tame" always implies a struggle and a victory. The thing being tamed was not easy to control — it had its own power, its own energy, its own resistance. To tame it required effort, skill, and persistence. This is why the word carries a sense of achievement when used in most contexts. Taming something is not a small feat.

It also always implies a change in nature, not just a temporary restraint. If you lock a wild animal in a cage, you have not tamed it — it is still wild, just imprisoned. But if you have truly tamed it, its relationship with humans has genuinely changed. It is now different from what it was. This is the key distinction: taming transforms.

To tame something is to take something wild, fierce, powerful, intense, or uncontrolled — whether it is an animal, a natural force, a human emotion, an abstract problem, or a difficult person — and bring it into a state where it is calm, controlled, and no longer a threat or a disruption. It always involves effort, patience, and a real transformation in the thing being tamed.
